title: Executive Presentation
narrative:
You're presenting to the executive team. The board wants to know why engineering is "behind schedule" and "over budget."

They have a spreadsheet with 47 columns. None of them understand technical debt, context switching, or the difference between a bug fix and a feature.

The VP of Sales just asked: "Why can't you just ship faster?"

choices.text: Tell the truth with data and analogies

success.text: You explain the situation with clear analogies and data. The executives finally understand. They adjust expectations and give you more resources.

failure.text: You get technical and lose them. The VP of Sales looks confused. The CEO says "I'll just ask the other departments to speed up."
failure.log: Lost the executives in technical detail.

choices.text: Promise more and hope you can deliver

success.text: You overpromise but find a way to deliver. It's stressful but you pull it off. The executives are happy. (For now.)

failure.text: You can't deliver on your promise. The executives lose trust in engineering. Future requests become more demanding.

success.text: You break down in tears. The room goes silent. Then a Mysterious Stranger from a consultancy company walks in, explains the situation to the executives, and sells them on a brand new way of working. The VP of Sales is consequently restructured. Nobody knows how this happened, but the bill from the consultancy is... substantial.
success.log: Cried in the boardroom. Consultancy saved the day? 🤷

failure.text: You start crying. It's not even a dramatic cry — just a quiet, confused weeping. The VP of Sales offers you a tissue and asks if you're okay. The CEO assumes you're having a medical episode and calls HR. The meeting is adjourned for 20 minutes while someone finds you a blanket. Nobody talks about it again.
failure.log: Cried in the boardroom. HR was called. 😭

title: Open Source Controversy
narrative:
Your company uses an open-source library that just had a major security vulnerability. The maintainer is one person who built it in their spare time over 5 years.

The board wants to: A) Replace the library entirely (risky, expensive) or B) Fork it and maintain it internally (legal minefield).

The maintainer just tweeted: "I can't maintain this anymore. I'm burned out."

You need to make a recommendation.

choices.text: Fund the maintainer to keep building it

success.text: You propose sponsoring the maintainer. The company agrees. The library gets a proper governance model. Everyone wins — including the entire open-source community.

failure.text: Legal blocks the sponsorship. "Liability concerns." The maintainer leaves. You're now responsible for a critical dependency.

choices.text: Start the migration to a replacement

success.text: You identify a viable alternative and create a migration plan. It's a year-long effort but the dependency risk is eliminated.

failure.text: No viable alternative exists. You've spent 3 months researching and there's nothing that matches the functionality. You're back to square one.

choices.text: Audit the fork's code quality yourself

success.text: Before the board meets, you audit the library: 14,000 lines, one author, but clean tests and a sane architecture. Forking is viable — the legal minefield is real but navigable. You hand the board a one-page risk map with the actual exposure numbers. Option B goes from "minefield" to "decision."
success.log: Audited the fork. The minefield became a map.

failure.text: You audit the code and find the real problem: the license has a clause that makes an internal fork a legal event, not an engineering one. Your audit is airtight and useless — this is now a law firm's problem, at law firm prices.
failure.log: The code was fine. The license wasn't.

title: The Great Hiring Freeze
narrative:
The company is "right-sizing." There's a hiring freeze. But your team's workload just doubled.

You have 5 people doing the work of 10. Deadlines are unrealistic. Morale is at an all-time low.

Your team lead asks: "How are we going to handle this?"

You're the senior person. They're looking to you.

choices.text: Prioritize ruthlessly and say no to everything else

success.text: You work with product to cut the scope in half. You protect your team from distraction. They deliver on the priorities. It's hard but sustainable.
success.log: Protected the team through the freeze!

failure.text: You try to do everything and so does your team. Everyone works weekends. Productivity drops because everyone is exhausted.

success.text: You identify automation opportunities. CI/CD improvements, automated testing, better tooling. The team becomes 2x more efficient.

failure.text: Automation projects take time to build. In the short term, productivity drops. The team is frustrated.

success.text: You spend two weeks building the pipeline that does the work of two of the missing ten: deploys, migrations, the weekly report. The team's load drops from impossible to merely heroic. The team lead says "this is why you're the senior person," and you both know it's the only reason the office is still standing.
success.log: Built the automation. Load: impossible → heroic.

failure.text: You build the automation, but it automates the process the PM is about to change. Two weeks of work becomes a cautionary tale about building before asking, and the team's load is still the work of ten.
failure.log: Automated a process that was about to change.

title: Boardroom Strategy Session
narrative:
For the first time, you're invited to the executive strategy meeting. The board wants engineering's input on a major business decision: acquire a competitor or build the features in-house.

The competitor has 50 engineers and a mature product. Building in-house would take 18 months and cost $5M.

The CEO asks: "What would you recommend?"

choices.text: Recommend acquisition — the tech is superior

success.text: You present a technical analysis. The board agrees. The acquisition goes through. You integrate the acquired product successfully.

failure.text: The acquired product has hidden technical issues. It's worse than expected. The integration costs 3x the budget.

success.text: You build it. It takes 18 months but the result is perfect for your needs. You have full IP ownership. The competitor is now irrelevant.
success.log: Built it and dominated the market!

failure.text: 18 months later, the market has moved on. The competitor launched 3 new features. Your "perfect" solution is already behind.
failure.log: Built it but lost the timing.

success.text: You come to the board meeting with a working prototype of the in-house path: the core feature, real data, real numbers on cost to scale. The 18-month estimate becomes a range with a floor. The board votes on evidence instead of vibes, and engineering's input is the tiebreaker.

failure.text: You build the prototype, but the board meeting is now, not next week. You present a two-week-old demo against a competitor that shipped a new feature yesterday. The prototype proves the concept and loses the quarter.
failure.log: The prototype was real. The timing wasn't.

title: The Data Breach
narrative:
It's 2 AM. Your phone buzzes.

"We've been breached. User data is exposed. The press is calling. The board wants answers."

You're the most senior engineer on call. This is your moment.

The breach was caused by an unpatched vulnerability in a library you recommended last month.

success.text: You lead the team through the night. You contain the breach, notify users, and work with legal. It's the hardest 12 hours of your career.

failure.text: You make a wrong call. The breach gets worse. The board is not happy.

choices.text: Delegate and let the security team handle it

success.text: You trust your security team. They handle it professionally. You focus on the technical response.

failure.text: The security team is overwhelmed. You should have stepped in. The breach spreads.

choices.text: Run the forensics — find how it happened

success.text: You pull the logs and trace the breach to the unpatched library — and to the config flag that disabled the patch. You find the exposure window: 6 hours, not the 6 days the first report claimed. The board's "answers" call becomes a containment story instead of a disaster story. The press gets a number, not a narrative.
success.log: 6 hours, not 6 days. The story changed.

failure.text: You trace the breach and find the real entry point was a second vulnerability, in code you reviewed. The forensics are flawless, which is exactly why they're devastating. The board's question is no longer "what happened" but "what do we do about it."
failure.log: The forensics pointed at your review.

title: The Board Presentation
narrative:
You're presenting to the board. They want to know the 5-year tech strategy.

You have a 30-minute slot. The board has 12 people. 8 of them don't know what a API is.

The CEO says: "Keep it simple. We want to know why we're spending $50M on engineering."

Your slides have architecture diagrams.

success.text: You explain tech strategy using restaurant analogies. The board understands. They approve the budget.

failure.text: The board is confused. The CEO asks "Why can't you just use NoSQL?" You don't know how to answer.

success.text: The CTO on the board loves it. They champion your proposal. Budget approved.
success.log: CTO on board loved the diagrams!

failure.text: The board falls asleep. The CEO asks if you can make it "easier to understand."

title: The Open Source Crisis
narrative:
Your company's flagship product uses an open-source library that just announced it's shutting down.

The maintainer is retiring. No successor. No fork.

Your product will break in 90 days. You have 3 options: rewrite, replace, or pray.

The board wants to know what's happening.

success.text: You lead a team to rewrite the dependency. It takes 6 months but you're self-sufficient now.

failure.text: The rewrite takes too long. The library shuts down. Your product breaks. Chaos ensues.

success.text: You find a better alternative. Migration takes 3 months. Your product is more stable now.

failure.text: No good replacement exists. You're stuck maintaining the old code.

success.text: You start the rewrite with a thin interface over the old library, so the product keeps running while the new core lands behind it. Ninety days later, the shutdown email is a non-event. The board asks what it cost. You tell them: one engineer, nine months of your reputation, and zero downtime.
success.log: Rewrote behind a facade. Zero downtime.

failure.text: You start the rewrite, but the old library's edge cases take weeks to surface — the maintainer knew things that were never documented. You're at day 40 of 90 and the product has a feature that only works on Tuesdays. The board wants an update. You give them one.
failure.log: The edge cases were never documented. Day 40.

title: The Company Merger
narrative:
Your company is merging with a competitor. Both have engineering teams. Both have different tech stacks.

The new CEO says: "We're keeping one stack. Figure out which one."

Your stack is newer but less battle-tested. Their stack is older but proven.

Both teams are nervous. Both want their stack to win.

success.text: You propose migrating gradually. Both teams contribute. The new system is better than either original.

failure.text: The CEO wants a clear winner. Your hybrid proposal is rejected. You're stuck in limbo.

success.text: You make a compelling case. Your stack wins. Your team is thrilled.

failure.text: Your stack loses. Your team is devastated. You're now maintaining their code.

choices.text: Map both codebases, find the real conflicts

success.text: You spend a week mapping both stacks: where they actually conflict, where they're compatible, where the "conflict" is political. You hand the new CEO a one-pager: 3 real integration points, 14 fake ones. The stack decision takes a meeting instead of a quarter, and both teams discover they disagree less than they thought.

failure.text: You map the codebases and find the real conflicts are in the data layer, which neither team wants to touch. Your map is perfect and the decision is postponed, because the honest answer is "this is harder than either of us wanted."
failure.log: The real conflict is in the data layer.

title: The Breaking API Change
narrative:
Your team's API just broke a major client's integration. You changed a response format without a deprecation period.

The client is furious. They're threatening to leave. Their CTO is calling your CEO.

Your team says: "It was just a small change! How bad could it be?"

You know how bad it could be.

success.text: You roll back, apologize sincerely, and offer a migration plan. The client stays. They respect your professionalism.

failure.text: The client has already moved on. They're switching to a competitor.

success.text: You build a compatibility layer in 48 hours. The client migrates at their pace. Everyone's happy.

failure.text: The compatibility layer has bugs. The client is even more frustrated.

success.text: You ship the compatibility layer before the client's CTO gets a second call: the old response format, generated from the new one, with a deprecation header and a 90-day clock. The client's fury cools to grudging respect. Their CTO calls your CEO to ask who wrote it, so they can send a thank-you.

failure.text: You write the shim, but the old format had an undocumented field the client's billing pipeline depends on. You find it in the shim's first week of logs. The client is saved, but now you own their billing edge cases, which is a new job you didn't apply for.
failure.log: The undocumented field. You now own their billing edge cases.

title: The Performance Crisis II
narrative:
Your platform is slow. Really slow. Average page load: 8 seconds. Users are complaining. Churn is up 15%.

You've been asked to "make it fast." No specifics. The CEO wants it "fixed by next sprint."

You open the profiler. The app makes 47 API calls per page load. Forty. Seven.

This is your final boss-level challenge.

success.text: You add Redis caching and reduce API calls from 47 to 3. Page load drops to 800ms. The CEO is thrilled.

failure.text: You cache aggressively but introduce stale data bugs. Now you have TWO problems.

success.text: You identify the rendering bottleneck and optimize it. Performance improves 5x.

failure.text: The bottleneck wasn't the frontend — it was the backend. You've optimized nothing.

choices.text: Profile and find the actual bottleneck

success.text: You profile the 47 API calls and find 41 of them are the same data, fetched 41 times. You fix the data layer, not the frontend: 8 seconds becomes 1.2. The CEO asks what it cost. One engineer, one week, and a graph that goes the right way.

failure.text: You profile and find the real bottleneck is the third-party analytics SDK, which the growth team refuses to remove. Your fix is correct, measured, and blocked by a org chart. The page loads in 7.9 seconds.
failure.log: The bottleneck is a SDK the growth team worships.

title: The Hiring Freeze II
narrative:
The company is "right-sizing." There's a hiring freeze. But your team's workload just doubled.

You have 5 people doing the work of 10. Deadlines are unrealistic. Morale is at an all-time low.

Your team lead asks: "How are we going to handle this?"

You're the senior person. They're looking to you.

choices.text: Prioritize ruthlessly and say no to everything else

success.text: You work with product to cut the scope in half. You protect your team from distraction. They deliver on the priorities.
success.log: Protected the team through the freeze!

failure.text: You try to do everything and so does your team. Everyone works weekends. Productivity drops.

success.text: You identify automation opportunities. CI/CD improvements, automated testing, better tooling. The team becomes 2x more efficient.

failure.text: Automation projects take time to build. In the short term, productivity drops.

success.text: You stop triaging and start building: the deploy pipeline, the migration runner, the status report that eats two meetings a week. The team's load drops from the work of ten to the work of six, which is still a lot, but people are smiling again.
success.log: Automated two meetings a week away.

failure.text: You build the automation in two weeks. The "right-sizing" ends in three, and the company hires back four of the ten — including the person whose job your pipeline did. The automation stays. The awkwardness stays longer.

title: BOSS: The Company-Wide Restructure
narrative:
Your FINAL BOSS. The company is restructuring. Teams are being merged. Reports are changing. The org chart is being redrawn.

You've spent 6 years building relationships, shipping products, and growing your career. Now everything is up in the air.

The new structure could make you a VP... or it could lay you off. Nobody knows yet.

This is it. Your career has led to this moment.

choices.text: Lead with transparency — share everything you know

success.text: Your transparency earns trust. You're offered a VP role leading the new engineering organization. You've reached the pinnacle of your career. Retirement? Or a new challenge?

failure.text: You share too much. Some information gets leaked. Management is unhappy. The restructuring is chaotic and you're left in limbo.

choices.text: Play it safe — say nothing and observe

success.text: You observe carefully, position yourself well, and land on your feet. You get a solid promotion. Not the top, but a great outcome.

failure.text: You play it too safe. You're left out of key decisions. When the new structure is announced, your role is eliminated.

choices.text: Start interviewing at the same time

success.text: Your network is strong. You have 3 offers on the table before the restructuring is even announced. You choose the best one.

failure.text: Interviews go poorly. The market is tough. You're still employed but unhappy. The restructuring leaves you in a worse position.
